title: No label
hook: many Jews today choose no movement at all

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: traditional. The traditional middle keeps the Friday night cup and the festivals, holding on to what was handed down. What did you do the way someone before you did it? Today, Jews who skip the label altogether. Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

A registration form for a Jewish summer camp. Name, age, allergies. Then a row of little boxes: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist, Other. A parent sits with the pen above the boxes for a long moment. The family lights candles most Fridays, goes to a different synagogue depending on who invites them, fasts on Yom Kippur, argues about Israel at dinner, and sends the kids to Hebrew school. None of the boxes fits. The parent ticks Other and writes, in small letters, just Jewish. Those two handwritten words are where today begins.
screen: `A ROW OF LITTLE BOXES.` → `NONE OF THEM FITS.` → `JUST JEWISH.`

segments.voice: No label. Go back to the people before the boxes. When the Israelites leave Egypt, the Torah says, "a mixed multitude went up also with them." There were no movement names on that road. The streams we have walked through in this block, from Orthodox to Humanistic, are real and serious, and they are also newer than the people. Then the covenant. Moses tells the people in Deuteronomy, "Neither with you only do I make this covenant and this oath," but also with those standing there and those not there that day. In that reading, the covenant comes before any membership list. Now the shape of a no-label life. Some Jews today belong to no movement at all. They may pray at an Orthodox synagogue on the High Holy Days, take a class at a Reform temple, join a friend's Shabbat dinner, and keep their own customs at home. Some call themselves just Jewish. Some are simply not interested in the question. Each of the movements would say it offers something a person shouldn't do without: a community, a teacher, a framework that holds when life gets hard. That is a fair point, and a no-label Jew may well agree with it and still not pick a box. Last, a line to keep the balance. Hillel taught, in the Mishnah, do not separate yourself from the community. No label is not the same as no people. A Jew without a movement can still be counted, still be welcomed, still belong. The label is optional. The belonging, in Hillel's view, is not.
screen: `A MIXED MULTITUDE.` · `A COVENANT BEFORE THE LIST.` · `A LITTLE OF EVERYTHING, AT HOME.` · `DON'T SEPARATE FROM THE COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `NO LABEL NEEDED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: describe your own practice without a label. Settle, and breathe. Silently, in three plain sentences, say what you actually do. Not what you call yourself, what you do. I light a candle on some evenings. I call my mother on Sundays. I sit with this lesson in the morning. Whatever is true. Then notice how it feels to be described by your actions instead of a box. Let the three sentences stand as they are, with no box around them. The bell holds the time.
No label. Jews who belong to no movement, who describe their practice in their own words, and who are still part of the people. Today's word.
Your line: no label needed. Today, when someone asks what you are, try answering with one thing you do instead. Day one thousand two hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Jews who choose no movement may attend different synagogues for different occasions, study and celebrate with friends, keep customs at home, and describe themselves as just Jewish.

notes: The outline says 'many Jews today choose no movement at all'; the lesson says 'some Jews' and avoids any statistic.
'The streams ... are newer than the people' is a general historical claim without dates; confirm.
Deuteronomy 29:14–15 is KJV verse numbering (Hebrew 29:13–14); confirm reference.
Avot 2:4 ('do not separate yourself from the community') is paraphrased and attributed to Hillel; confirm.
